newsitem.title: USA: Oil, wheat lead prices lower in U.S. trading.
newsitem.headline: Oil, wheat lead prices lower in U.S. trading.

text.p: Oil prices tumbled Friday as traders bet forecasts for milder weather in the Northeast would curtail demand for heating oil.
Gold and silver prices and wheat also ended lower. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures fell 1.58 points to 238.99.
Weather Services Corp. forecast that temperatures in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market, would moderate to normal to slightly above normal next week.

"At first, we had forecasts for below normal temperatures but now they are saying it's going to be normal to above normal next week," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.
Heating oil for February delivery lost 1.69 cents to 68.65 cents a gallon and February gasoline fell 1.35 cents to 68.47 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Friday was also the final trading day for the February contracts, which prompted volatile trading in the session.
March crude oil fell 72 cents to $24.15 a barrel.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, a wave of selling by professional speculators drove wheat futures to new contract lows. March wheat fell 10-1/2 cents to $3.59-3/4 a bushel after setting a new contract low at $3.57.
Prompting the sell-off was widespread talk that Egypt and India, expected to be in the market soon to buy wheat, were ignoring U.S. grain due to high prices.
"There's potentially up to 2 million tons of business around here and the U.S. isn't going to get any of it. U.S. prices are too high," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist of FIMAT Futures.
Hard red wheat at U.S. Gulf of Mexico ports was quoted at about $174 a metric ton, compared to $142 for Argentine wheat ready for loaading at the Plate River.
Corn was pulled lower by the selling in wheat, with March corn losing 3-1/2 cents to $2.70-1/4 a bushel. Traders also pointed to growing export competition.
South Korea on Friday bought 36,000 tons of corn from China, which may export another 200,000 to 300,000 tons soon, after being a major importer last year.
Fresh rains in Brazilian soybean regions continued to douse any worries about crop problems there before harvest. March soybeans fell 3-1/4 cents to $7.38-1/4 a bushel.

Precious metals prices fell for the fourth straight day with gold and platinum sliding to new three-year lows. April gold closed $1.50 an ounce lower at $346 and March silver lost 3.5 cents to $4.92 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.

"Sentiment in precious metals is extremely poor, though volumes were not that heavy today," FIMAT New York trader John Tyree said. "Both the funds and bullion banks were selling today, with talk of European central bank sales still around."

On Thursday gold fell sharply on renewed talk of European central bank sales and fears that the U.S. government's successful new issue of inflation-indexed bonds removed the need for gold as an inflation hedge for U.S. investors.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee closed mixed as the market awaited data on positions of large traders from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
March coffee fell 0.90 cent to 139.4 cents a pound, but was still up about 40 percent in the last two months on worries about tight supplies and the new crop in Brazil, the world's largest producer.

"The speculators have done some profit taking, but they are still overextended," said Rich Wistisen, vice president of analysis at Commodity Information. "If the CFTC show a huge increase in spec longs, it could spark more profit taking."
